title: Evergine binding manifest
description: Declares where a binding's upstream specification lives, how it is generated and what it publishes. Read by both the deterministic reusable workflows and the agentic workflows.
$comment: package and generator are required together rather than always, so a repository that has an upstream to track but produces no NuGet package can carry a manifest. EvergineTeam/JoltPhysicsC is the case: it is the C wrapper JoltPhysics.NET binds to, has no C# generator of its own, and needs release resolution from this machinery rather than a second implementation of it.

toolbox.description: Toolbox version this manifest was written against. The toolbox-updater compares it with the current release to decide whether a manifest migration is needed.

project.description: Path to the binding .csproj, relative to the repository root.

runtime-identifier.description: RID passed to the build, e.g. win-x64. Empty means portable.

wrapper.description: For a repository that is a hand-maintained C wrapper over a C++ library rather than a generated binding. Read by cpp-wrapper-porter.

profile.description: Path to this repository's wrapper profile, which decides everything docs/cpp-wrapper-conventions.md deliberately leaves open: identifier scheme, overload policy, scope contract, how to apply a bump, how to run the tests. Required rather than inferred -- reading a codebase tells you what it does, not which of its habits are decisions, and guessing produces code that looks native and is not.

version-macro.description: Name of the macro stating the upstream version this wrapper targets, kept in step with release.current. Without one, a downstream binding can only answer 'which upstream is this?' by cloning two repositories and resolving a commit against a tag list.

kind.description: Adapter used to fetch the specification. See docs/adapters/. vendored: nothing fetches it, because nothing can -- the sources sit in the repository because obtaining them needs a sign-in or a licence acceptance. Declare version-probe so the version is read out of the sources rather than maintained by hand.

version-probe.description: For kind: vendored. Reads the upstream version out of a file already in the tree, because there is no tag or release API to ask. Each pattern must match exactly once; zero matches is an error rather than a silent fall back to the recorded value, since a silent miss would report the old version for as long as nobody looked.

file.description: Path to the vendored file that carries the version.

patterns.description: Regular expressions, each with one capture group and each matching exactly once. Several are allowed because a version is not always written in one place: Vuforia spells it as three separate #defines.

join.description: String used to join the captures into a version.

language.description: Language the upstream project is written in (c, cpp, rust, zig, ...). Informational: it tells the agent what kind of source it is reasoning about. The binding output is always C#.

project.description: Home of the upstream project. Used to look up releases and derive the upstream version.

version-from.description: How to determine which upstream version the vendored spec corresponds to.

bump.description: For kind: git-submodule. report-only (default): compare the recorded pointer against upstream and stop, because moving it means rebuilding native binaries. together: move every submodule to its upstream head as one set, so a binding whose submodules compile into a single library never lands a combination upstream never built.

release.description: Follow tagged releases instead of a branch. A binding that ships native binaries needs this: the header and the libraries have to come from the same revision, and a branch is a moving target.

track.description: stable: the newest published non-prerelease release, as decided by the upstream author. latest: the newest release including prereleases. pinned: stay on `current` until a human moves it.

current.description: Tag currently vendored. Rewritten by binding-fetch-upstream when it brings in a newer release, so this is the single place the version lives.

repo.description: owner/name to read releases from. Defaults to the repo of the first source that declares one.

assets.description: Binaries published as assets of the release the sources come from, unpacked into this repository. Orthogonal to `kind`: a binding can take its headers out of a repository tree and its native libraries from a release of that same repository, which is the case this exists for. Use it when the libraries are built elsewhere -- natives-artifact-pattern on the CD covers the case where they are built in the same run. Two alternatives were rejected: artifacts expire and carry no version, and calling the other repository's build as a reusable workflow cannot follow a resolved tag, because `uses:` takes no expression. Destinations are reported as fetched sources, so a rebuilt library does not read as a changed API.

name.description: Asset name, or a glob matching several. Fails when nothing matches, because a manifest asking for libraries that are not published means the package would ship without them.

repo.description: owner/name to read the release from. Defaults to release.repo.

tag.description: Release tag to read. Defaults to the tag release tracking resolved, which is what keeps the libraries and the headers on one revision.

unpack.description: Treat the asset as an archive and extract it. Omit to write the asset itself. Member names are validated: an entry escaping the destination is refused.

into.description: Directory the contents land in, relative to the repository root. An archive that already carries runtimes/<rid>/native/ needs only the package directory here, so unpacking is the whole mapping.

sources.description: One entry per file or tree that feeds the generator.

url.description: Direct download URL. Required for kind: http-file.

repo.description: owner/name of the upstream repository. Required for kind: git-tree and git-submodule.

ref.description: Branch, tag or SHA to read from. For kind: git-tree, either this or an upstream.release block must supply one; an explicit ref here wins, so a manifest can pin one source while the rest follow the tracked release.

remote-path.description: Path inside the upstream repository. Required for kind: git-tree.

path.description: Destination path in this repository, relative to the root. For kind: git-submodule this is the mount point.

exports.description: For kind: git-submodule. Files to copy out of the submodule after bumping it -- typically the generated definitions the code generator reads. Because they come from the submodule rather than being fetched separately, the definitions and the binaries built from that same revision cannot disagree. Their destinations are reported as fetched sources, not generator output.

to.description: Destination in this repository, relative to the root.

format.description: How the file must be parsed. Decoupled from `language` on purpose: a Rust project exposing a C API is language: rust, format: c-header.

project.description: Path to the generator .csproj, relative to the repository root.

name.description: Generator/binding name, matching the generator-name input of the reusable workflows.

output.description: Directories the generator writes into. Agents treat everything under these paths as generated output and everything outside them as hand-written. A list rather than a single path because some repositories generate into several folders that sit alongside hand-written source -- ImGui.Net writes four, next to files like Types.cs that must not be touched. Keep these paths as narrow as the truth allows: naming a parent folder that also holds hand-written code tells the agent it may overwrite it.

agents.description: Per-repository overrides for the agentic workflows. Every field is optional; omitting the block accepts the toolbox defaults.

model.description: Copilot model id. Overrides the toolbox default for this repository.

max-ai-credits.description: Hard spending ceiling for a single run, in GitHub AI Credits (1 credit = $0.01).
